claim: A nineteen-year-old undergraduate student from Najafgarh, named in the reporting, is reported to have lost vision in his right eye after fragments struck the eye during the police action of 20 July 2026, perforating the cornea; a second operation on 31 July 2026 inserted a lens and vision had not returned; not all fragments were removed.
notes: Recorded because the pellet question on this record has until now been a dispute between a police denial and a medical category. This is the injury itself, with a date, a procedure and an outcome. It does not establish what was fired: a perforating fragment injury is consistent with more than one munition, and INC-DEL-005 stays disputed. It is the reason the question is worth the work. He is named in every source cited and has spoken publicly under his own name; this archive still does not reproduce the name, on the same rule applied to the complainant at PROC-DEL-003, because a record that outlives the news cycle should not be the thing that keeps a medical fact about a private person searchable. The name is one click away in the sources, and the decision to follow it belongs to him.

claim: Mumbai Police registered 13 First Information Reports between 18 and 22 July 2026 against more than 400 people for taking part in protests over the NEET examination without police permission, at Shivaji Park, Chaityabhoomi, Chembur and Shiv Sena Bhavan, on charges reported as unlawful assembly, disobedience of an order duly promulgated by a public servant and wrongful restraint; those named were served notices and released, the offences being bailable and carrying a maximum of two years.
notes: This closes INC-MAH-001 and PUB-MAH-001, which have read UNKNOWN since 15 August, and it closes them with an answer nobody was looking for. The archive held open a Maharashtra shell on the strength of a Supreme Court petition saying disturbances had spread there, and went looking for a lathi charge. What is on the record instead is thirteen FIRs against four hundred people for assembling without permission. No use of force in Maharashtra is established here and none is alleged in these sources. That distinction is the finding and the record keeps it: the shell is filled with what happened. It also puts Maharashtra in the same class as Kochi, Kolkata and Assam, and Patna sits in a different class; the class with Maharashtra is the one where a document with an author exists, because a refusal of permission and an FIR are both written by somebody.

claim: Ernakulam Town South police registered a case on its own motion against 101 people, the musician Hirandas Murali, who performs as Vedan, his manager Vignesh G. Pillai, and 99 others, over a solidarity gathering held near Central Park, Panampilly Nagar, Kochi at about 5 pm on Wednesday 22 July 2026 in support of the student protests in Delhi, under sections 190, 223 and 285 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. The First Information Report is reported to state that the organisers went ahead after being served a notice refusing permission.
notes: Kerala was not on this archive before today. It is here for one reason, and it is the reason the whole site exists: the FIR says a notice refusing permission was served. That notice is a written order. It has a date, a signatory, an office and a file, and unlike a lathi charge it cannot have happened without leaving one. The question this archive asks of a baton is unanswerable because a baton leaves no paper; asked of a refusal of permission it is answerable by an RTI application to a named police station. No use of force is established at Kochi and none is alleged in these sources. The three sections carry the archive's standing caution on statute: they are quoted as the reports give them and have not been checked against the current text by anyone who practises.

claim: Seven cases were registered in Kolkata over the student protests, with about 70 persons identified, reported on 28 July 2026, on which date the West Bengal government's decision on withdrawal was reported as still pending. The state is reported to have said there would be no coercive action in cases registered up to 6 pm on 26 July 2026.
notes: Recorded as evidence and NOT opened as an incident shell. There is no located place, no date of any police action and no account of force: what is established is that seven files exist and about seventy people are named in them. That is not enough to open a record called an incident, and the archive has refused on this ground before: Sitamarhi was left unopened on a single account for the same reason. If the location and date of a Kolkata action are established, or the seven case numbers obtained, this becomes a shell. Until then it is a fact about a police force's paperwork, which is worth holding and is not the same thing.

claim: Five cases were registered in Assam over the student protests and 13 people arrested, reported on 28 July 2026; the Assam government issued a notification stating that the process of withdrawing the registered cases would be initiated as per law promptly, and that those arrested would be released.
notes: Recorded as evidence and NOT opened as an incident shell, on the same reasoning as INC-WB-001: no place, no date, no account of force. What makes it worth holding is the notification. A state withdrawing criminal cases does it by a written instrument that names an office and carries a date, and it is obtainable by RTI from the Assam Home Department in a way that a decision to charge never is. Bihar issued one on the same day and the two were shown to the CJP delegation together. Note the units before comparing states: Bihar is reported at 694 detained and 355 booked, Assam at 13 arrested and 5 cases, Mumbai at 400 booked and 13 FIRs, Kolkata at about 70 in 7 cases. People booked, people arrested, people detained and cases registered are four different counts and the reporting moves between them.

claim: 694 people are reported to have been detained in Bihar over the student protests and 355 booked; the Bihar Home Department issued a notification, reported on 28 July 2026, withdrawing the cases and stating that no adverse legal action shall be taken against protesters in respect of matters before 6 pm on 26 July 2026, with those in custody to be released.
notes: The largest set of figures the archive holds for Bihar, and the first that comes from the state itself. It does not contradict the 64 FIRs the PUCL hearing reported at INC-BIH-005: an FIR can name many people, so 355 booked in an unstated number of files and 64 FIRs are not two answers to one question. The cut-off is the part to keep. A withdrawal expressed as a time on a date, 6 pm on 26 July, is drawn from a file, and the file is obtainable from the Bihar Home Department. It is also the same cut-off West Bengal is reported to have used, which is worth knowing when asking either state where the line came from.

claim: On Friday 2 October 2026 Delhi Police detained several hundred people who were trying to reach Jantar Mantar to demand the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. The counts differ by source and the archive holds no official statement of any of them. Al Jazeera reports over 500 by about 3 pm. Deccan Chronicle reports over 500, with one official first giving 150 and another about 500. The Week and Outlook report over 700, Outlook attributing the figure to police officials. ThePrint, in its report of 3 October, says approximately 1,000 people were detained on the Friday. Hindustan Times, as carried by Outlook, is reported to give about 1,000 across Delhi: nearly 750 near Jantar Mantar and about 400 elsewhere, with around 200 held under house arrest beforehand. Reuters describes batches of student protesters put onto buses and taken away. Those detained are reported to include opposition political leaders and members of the student organisations AISA, SFI and NSUI.
notes: The figures differ but may not conflict: 500 by mid-afternoon, 700 and about 1,000 by the end of the day are consistent with each other, and most sources do not say when each count was taken. The components reported for the Hindustan Times figure do not sum to 1,000 as they are summarised, which is a reason to read the original before quoting it. The archive records every figure and does not choose. Detention under a prohibitory order is not a finding of force, and this record makes none. Outlook reports Delhi Police, the Rapid Action Force and the CRPF at the site, and quotes a Delhi Police officer putting the deployment at more than 1,000 personnel; its later report, citing Hindustan Times, says more than 5,000. Al Jazeera reports at least 11 metro stations closed; Deccan Chronicle says 12. Al Jazeera takes its figures from Reuters and The Times of India, so it is not independent of them; the others are separate reports.

sources.originates_from: Reuters and The Times of India, as cited in the article
PTI and Delhi Police officials, as cited in the article
Hindustan Times, as cited in the article

claim: A prohibitory order under section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 was in force across New Delhi district on 2 October 2026. Al Jazeera, citing The Times of India, says it barred gatherings of more than five people, slogans, speeches and protest activity. Outlook says it restricted gatherings of five or more people without permission.
notes: Three outlets report that the order existed. They word its scope slightly differently ("more than five" and "five or more"), and the archive holds no copy of the order, so the wording is a report of it. The order is a written instrument with a date, an issuing office and a text, which is what separates it from the force question on INC-0001. Who issued it is recorded separately at INC-DEL-013. The section number is quoted as the reports give it and has not been checked against the current text of the Sanhita by anyone who practises.

sources.originates_from: Reuters and The Times of India, as cited in the article

claim: The sources disagree on which office issued the section 163 order of 2 October 2026. Al Jazeera, citing The Times of India, says Delhi Police imposed it. Outlook says it was issued by the Delhi government.
notes: Not resolved here. The two answers lead to different custodians and different RTI routes: Delhi Police sits under the Union Home Ministry, while the Delhi government is a separate public authority. Neither source quotes the order or names a signatory. See OQ-055. A further Outlook report, citing Hindustan Times, says Delhi Police imposed the restrictions on the Friday morning, which sits with the Al Jazeera account and against Outlook's own earlier statement that the Delhi government issued the order. The dispute stays open until the order is read.

sources.originates_from: Reuters and The Times of India, as cited in the article
Hindustan Times, as cited in the article

claim: Outlook reports that protesters alleged they were dragged along the road and beaten with batons during the detentions of 2 October 2026, and that a history student from Miranda House reported bruises. Reuters, as carried by Al Jazeera and The Kathmandu Post, reports protesters shoved and bundled onto buses, and says police prevented gatherings without describing other physical force.
notes: These are allegations made by protesters, reported by one outlet, beside a wire report that describes shoving and no more. The archive does not hold footage, a medical record or a police account. None of the articles read for this entry mentions tear gas, pellets or firearms; that is an absence in those articles, and it says nothing about whether any were used. See OQ-060.

sources.originates_from: Reuters and The Times of India, as cited in the article

claim: Outlook, Deccan Chronicle and India TV (as carried by tob.news) report that internet services were suspended in the Jantar Mantar area on 2 October 2026. Outlook says for several hours. None of the three gives the hours, the area or the issuing office.
notes: Three outlets report the suspension; none quotes an order. One headline in the 3 October sweep reports the cut ran until 9 pm, but the page was not retrieved and the figure is not recorded here. The July order recorded at INC-DEL-007 shows the form such an order takes and which office signs it, and a suspension order is the kind of instrument the Supreme Court has said must be published (see PREC-SHUT-001). Whether a separate order was made on 2 October, and by whom, is OQ-056. India TV is the origin of the tob.news report and is not independent of it.

claim: The Week reports that an independent journalist accused an Assistant Commissioner of Police of hitting her on the chest while she filmed the detention of a student leader on 2 October 2026, and that she waited over three hours at a police station without an FIR being registered. It reports complaints from three women alleging sexual offences during the protest of 2 and 3 October, which the New Delhi district transferred to the Crime Branch at Kamla Market, and three FIRs registered over the protest in which no individual or organisation was named as an accused. The Cockroach Janta Party is reported to have demanded an FIR against the officer by noon on 4 October.
notes: One source for all of it. The officer is named in the source and not here, on the rule the archive applies to a private person and to an unproven allegation: holding a post is not evidence of having done what is alleged. The complaints are allegations and are recorded as such. The Week's text says "sexual assault" while its address says "sexual harassment", so the nature of the complaints is not settled by the source. No complainant is named in the source or here. See OQ-057. Later reporting is recorded at INC-DEL-022: PTI and Deccan Chronicle report that the complaints were of sexual harassment, that no FIR was registered when the journalists went to a police station, and that the New Delhi district transferred the complaints to the Crime Branch for a fair and impartial enquiry. The Week describes the first allegation as a blow to the chest; PTI quotes the complaint as alleging sexual assault. The two wordings are different allegations and neither is resolved here. The three FIRs are recorded at INC-DEL-017.

claim: Mumbai Police registered a First Information Report at Shivaji Park police station on 3 October 2026 over the Cockroach Janta Party gathering held at Shivaji Park on Friday 2 October 2026 against the organisers and 400 to 500 unidentified supporters, under sections 189 and 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita read with sections 37(1)(3) and 135 of the Maharashtra Police Act. The gathering demanded the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner over the Special Intensive Revision. All three sources report that police had refused permission. ANI, as carried by Asianet News, gives the stated ground as a Bombay High Court judgment in PIL 116/2009 dated 4 January 2013 and a later Maharashtra government order. No arrests are reported.
notes: The same class of record as INC-MAH-002: a case registered for assembling without permission, with no use of force established and none alleged in these sources. A refusal of permission is a written instrument with a date and a signatory, and the FIR is a second one; both can be asked for (OQ-059, FQ-022). The Free Press Journal also reports an altercation between supporters and a group opposing the demonstration after the gathering ended, with police intervening; that is one source and is not a finding about the police. The Supreme Court order of 1 September 2026 recorded at PROC-SC-014 is reported to cover FIRs over the protests of 20 to 25 July; this is a different gathering, and the archive draws no conclusion about how the order bears on it. The sections are quoted as the reports give them and have not been checked against the current text by anyone who practises. Who is named and who complained is DISPUTED at INC-MAH-004.

claim: The three sources read for the Mumbai FIR of 3 October 2026 disagree on who it names and who made the complaint. PTI, as carried by The Tribune, identifies one organiser, Abhijeet Dipke, and says the complaint came from a private resident of the Shivaji Park area and is not a case registered on the police's own motion. ANI, as carried by Asianet News, names four organisers (Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka, Saurav Das and Ratna Singh) and says the complaint was made by an advocate living in the area. The Free Press Journal names two (Abhijeet Dipke and Ajinkya Shinde) and says an advocate filed a separate complaint.
notes: Not resolved here, and not resolvable from reporting: the FIR is the document that settles it. The three accounts agree that Abhijeet Dipke is named. Whether the case rests on a private complaint or was registered by the police is a real difference, because it changes which office to ask. The complainant is a private person and is not named in this record. See OQ-058.

claim: Three FIRs were registered on 3 October 2026 over the protest of 2 October at Jantar Mantar, at Parliament Street and Connaught Place police stations. Outlook, citing Hindustan Times, reports the charge as section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, disobedience of an order promulgated by a public servant. ThePrint, citing PTI and Delhi Police officials, reports sections 223(a), 221, 132 and 3(5). Both report that no individual or organisation is named in the accused column, Outlook quoting a police officer.
notes: Two reports with different origins (Hindustan Times and PTI) agree on the number, the offences of disobedience and no named accused, and differ in how many sections they list. The FIRs themselves would settle it. Outlook says organisers and participating organisations are mentioned in the FIRs even though none is named as accused. The sections are quoted as the reports give them and have not been checked against the current text by anyone who practises. This supersedes the single-source mention of three FIRs at INC-DEL-016.

sources.originates_from: Hindustan Times, as cited in the article
PTI and Delhi Police officials, as cited in the article

claim: ThePrint, citing PTI and Delhi Police officials, reports that nearly 200 protesters were detained on Saturday 3 October 2026 as AISA and others returned to Jantar Mantar the day after the mass detentions, among them the AISA president, a civil society activist, a senior advocate and student volunteers from the AAP student wing. The student wing alleged that some volunteers were detained and taken around different parts of Delhi in a bus for several hours before being taken to Jafarpur police station.
notes: One outlet for the figure and for the allegation. ThePrint carried an earlier version of the same story with a figure of around 150, so the count moved during the day. The bus allegation is made by a political organisation and is not corroborated here. Section 163 BNSS is described as in force on the Friday; the sources read do not say whether it was extended to Saturday.

sources.originates_from: PTI and Delhi Police officials, as cited in the article

claim: The News Mill reports, on police sources, that around 15 Delhi Police personnel were injured, some women personnel reportedly by bites, and around 110 people were detained when the Indian Youth Congress marched from Raisina Road towards Jantar Mantar on a Sunday. The page carries no police statement on its own account.
notes: The police account of injuries to police is recorded because it is part of what happened and because an account that holds only protesters' allegations would be one-sided. One outlet, anonymous police sources, no statement on the record. The date is not settled by this source: the page was read as dating the protest to Sunday 5 October, and 5 October 2026 is a Monday; the Sunday of that weekend is 4 October. The archive has not corrected the source and records the date as the Sunday after 3 October.

claim: Delhi Police refused permission for the protest planned at Jantar Mantar on 2 October 2026. DT Next reports it on unnamed police sources and says the protest was called by AISA, a Rajya Sabha member and a Supreme Court lawyer. Deccan Chronicle reports police saying permission had not been granted and the AAP saying letters seeking it were sent about a week earlier. Bar and Bench reports a Delhi Police order dated 1 October 2026 rejecting the Indian Youth Congress application for permission to demonstrate there.
notes: The Indian Youth Congress order of 1 October is a written instrument with a date, and the Youth Congress has put it before the Delhi High Court (PROC-DEL-005), so a copy exists outside the police. It is the Delhi counterpart of the Maharashtra refusal at INC-MAH-003 and the Kochi notice at INC-KER-001. None of the sources names the officer or office that signed it. See OQ-061 and FQ-023.

claim: IBTimes India reports that Delhi Police personnel at the Jantar Mantar protests did not wear name tags, that junior personnel were allowed to remove them while most IPS officers kept theirs, and that officials gave the reason as preventing individual officers being identified and targeted on social media after the protest of 20 July, with junior personnel assured that no action would follow if they acted within the law.
notes: One outlet. Hindustan Times and The Times of India headlines in the 5 October sweep carry the same story and were not retrieved. The record matters to this archive for a plain reason: an officer who cannot be identified cannot be asked who gave an order, and the explanation offered concerns harassment of officers and their families, which is a real harm and is recorded as the police's stated reason and not as the archive's view.

claim: PTI and Deccan Chronicle report that three women journalists alleged sexual harassment by police personnel during the Jantar Mantar protest of 3 October 2026, that no FIR was registered when they went to a police station, and that Delhi Police transferred the complaints to the Crime Branch for what an unnamed New Delhi district officer called a fair and impartial enquiry. PTI reports that the Crime Branch said it would examine the allegations and record statements, and that the Press Club of India expressed concern and urged immediate action.
notes: The complainants are not named here. PTI reports that an Assistant Commissioner of Police is named in the complaint and could not be reached for comment; the officer is not named in this record, on the rule that an unproven allegation does not put a name in the archive. Deccan Chronicle reports that protesters and opposition figures say police cited the Crime Branch inquiry as the reason for deferring an FIR. Whether an FIR has since been registered is OQ-057. This is the same set of complaints The Week reports at INC-DEL-016, in different words.

claim: Bar and Bench reports that the president of the Indian Youth Congress moved the Delhi High Court on 3 October 2026 against Delhi Police's order of 1 October 2026 rejecting the organisation's application for permission to protest against the Chief Election Commissioner at Jantar Mantar. PTI, as carried by Deccan Chronicle, reports that on Friday 9 October 2026 a bench of Acting Chief Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and Justice Sanjay Sharma declined an urgent hearing, with the Acting Chief Justice asking what the urgency was, and said the matter would be listed on Monday 12 October. The same report says the organisation had applied on 25 September for 100 to 150 people from 1 to 25 October, and that the petition asks the Court to quash the police communication of 1 October and direct fresh consideration of the request.
notes: Two outlets with different origins report the petition and the order of 1 October. The case number is not reported in either. No order on the merits exists yet. The hearing of 12 October is a date to check. Retrieving the petition and the order of 1 October is FQ-023. 14 October 2026: the 12 October hearing happened and is recorded at PROC-DEL-006. The matter was deferred to 13 October; that day's outcome is not yet found. 15 October 2026: on 13 October the Court issued notice and listed the matter for 17 November; the police say the plea is infructuous after Jantar Mantar was denotified (PROC-DEL-008, PROC-DEL-007).

claim: LiveLaw reports that on 5 October 2026 a bench headed by the Chief Justice of India, Surya Kant, agreed to list a plea seeking directions to Delhi Police to permit peaceful protests at Jantar Mantar, titled Priya Mishra v. Union of India, Diary No. 62121/2026. The Chief Justice is quoted as saying that if similar matters are pending the Court will find out, and that it will only list the matter.
notes: One source retrieved. Other outlets carry the story and were not read. Listing is not a hearing and no order on the merits is recorded. The petition and any order are to be retrieved from the Court's own site, as for FQ-016 and FQ-018.

claim: The Tribune reports that on Tuesday 6 October 2026 about 300 opposition MPs marched from Parliament towards the Election Commission headquarters, that police stopped the march near NITI Aayog, and that several leaders were detained.
notes: One outlet, and the account of the first day is a summary inside a report about the second. The Wire carries a report headlined as Delhi Police detaining Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi during the INDIA bloc protest, but only its headline could be read, so it is not cited for anything here. The Election Commission is reported elsewhere to have said no party had sought an appointment before the march; that is not recorded here because the page carrying it was not read.

claim: On Wednesday 7 October 2026 Delhi Police detained opposition leaders near Jantar Mantar, among them Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra. The Tribune and Siasat both report that Rahul Gandhi was taken to Barakhamba Road police station and released within hours, and report that Priyanka Gandhi was taken to Chhatrasal Stadium. The Tribune reports that police stopped three buses carrying MPs near the Janpath and Ashoka Road crossing for nearly two hours, and that other detained leaders included Deepender Singh Hooda and Derek O'Brien. Siasat reports that security personnel told protesters that section 163 was in force.
notes: Two outlets agree on who was detained, where they were taken and that they were released the same day. Neither quotes a police statement. Siasat's wording is 'BNS 163', which is the section of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and not of the Nyaya Sanhita; the archive records it as section 163 and has not corrected the source. Whether an order was in force on 7 October, and whether it is the order of 2 October recorded at INC-DEL-012, is part of OQ-055.

sources.originates_from: PTI inputs, as stated in the article

claim: The Tribune reports that Priyanka Gandhi Vadra said police assaulted protesters and that she had been scratched and thrown to the ground, that Mahua Moitra alleged protesters were manhandled and accused police of using force, and that Jairam Ramesh said leaders were dragged away. The report carries no statement from Delhi Police.
notes: These are allegations by named politicians, reported as theirs. The Tribune also reports that women police personnel removed Priyanka Gandhi Vadra from the road where she was lying down, which is the police side of the same event and is not an allegation. No footage, medical record or police account is held.

claim: Siasat, with PTI inputs, refers to an FIR registered against Rahul Gandhi, which Akhilesh Yadav is reported to have tied to the protest of Tuesday 6 October 2026. The article gives no police station, no sections and no complainant, and quotes no police statement.
notes: The FIR is mentioned in a photo caption and in a politician's remark, and the article does not describe it. A search result summarised it as an FIR for entering Akashvani Bhawan without permission; the page read does not say that, and the archive does not record it. See OQ-062.

sources.originates_from: PTI inputs, as stated in the article

claim: FIR No. 110/2016 was registered at Police Station Vasant Kunj North, Delhi, over the event held at Jawaharlal Nehru University on 9 February 2016. The Delhi High Court order of 2 March 2016 records it as registered under Sections 124-A and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, and records the State's status report as saying the case was by then under investigation under Sections 124-A, 120-B, 34, 147 and 149.

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Delhi High Court order of 2 March 2016, Kanhaiya Kumar v. State (NCT of Delhi), W.P.(Crl.) 558/2016
sources.originates_from: Delhi High Court (Pratibha Rani J.); the court's own copy was not fetched

sources.originates_from: Supreme Court of India daily orders; the court's own copy on sci.gov.in was not fetched

notes: Both orders name the FIR number and station. The registration date is not stated in either order; the High Court order says in paragraph 27 that the FIR 'has been registered only about three weeks back'. LiveLaw (14 January 2019) gives 11 February 2016 as the registration date, a single secondary source (see HIST-JNU16-002). Sedition is the label the FIR carries; no finding on the merits is recorded here, and the High Court order itself says its observations are not an expression on merits.

claim: The FIR was registered on 11 February 2016 against unidentified persons following complaints from a Member of Parliament of the BJP (named in the report as Maheish Girri) and from the ABVP, under Sections 124A and 120B of the Indian Penal Code.
notes: Single secondary source, published 14 January 2019, describing the chargesheet. The complainant detail is not in the two court orders read for this file. A different account is recorded by the State in the High Court (HIST-JNU16-003): that the FIR followed a Zee News telecast of 10 February and raw footage obtained from the channel. Both accounts may be true. The archive has not seen the FIR itself. Obtain the FIR text (Delhi Police publishes FIRs online in many cases; check) to settle complainant and date.

claim: In the Delhi High Court on 2 March 2016 the Additional Solicitor General for the State submitted that: permission for a cultural evening at Sabarmati Dhaba, JNU, on 9 February 2016 had been granted on 8 February; JNU authorities cancelled it on learning of posters about Afzal Guru and Maqbool Bhatt; the Chief Security Officer of JNU and the local police were informed; local police and security staff positioned themselves between two groups of students; and, after a Zee News telecast on 10 February 2016, raw footage was obtained from the channel and FIR No. 110/2016 was registered. The order records this as the State's submission.

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Delhi High Court order of 2 March 2016, Kanhaiya Kumar v. State (NCT of Delhi), W.P.(Crl.) 558/2016
sources.originates_from: Delhi High Court (Pratibha Rani J.); the court's own copy was not fetched

notes: VERIFIED only as to what the order records the State as having submitted. The order does not find these facts. It also records the petitioner's contrary account (that he raised no anti-national slogans, that the campus stayed peaceful, and that the video was reported to be doctored) in paragraphs 7 to 9, and the Standing Counsel for the Government of NCT of Delhi saying the petitioner could be released on bail (paragraph 25). This is the only primary document read that describes who informed the police before 12 February; it describes a call to police on 9 February and says nothing about an order to enter the campus on 12 February.

claim: Kanhaiya Kumar, president of the JNU Students' Union, was arrested by Delhi Police on 12 February 2016 in connection with the sedition case, and was in police custody until 17 February 2016 and in judicial custody until 2 March 2016.

sources.originates_from: Supreme Court committee report, as quoted via LiveLaw

notes: The Quint (16 February 2016) and The News Minute (25 February 2016) are independent outlets. The Delhi High Court order of 2 March 2016 (paragraph 8) records the petitioner's submission that he had been remanded to police custody three times; it does not give the arrest date. Whether the arrest took place on campus, and in what manner, is covered at HIST-JNU16-005.

claim: Delhi Police went onto the JNU campus on 12 February 2016 and took Kanhaiya Kumar into custody there.

sources.originates_from: JNU status report to the HRD ministry, as reported

notes: The claim is widely repeated, but no source fetched for this file states the place, time and manner of the arrest in terms. The Quint (20 February 2016) says the Vice-Chancellor was criticised for not following protocol before police were allowed onto the campus, and gives no date. Onmanorama (15 February 2016) reports a JNU status report saying a letter was sent to police asking them to take utmost precautions before entering the campus, and that police told the university they would enter only if absolutely necessary. Search-result snippets, which were not read as pages, describe a plainclothes arrest from the campus and raids on hostels on 12 and 13 February; they are not relied on. Not found: a police arrest memo, the case diary entry, or a court record of the place of arrest.

claim: A letter from the JNU Registrar is reported by The Quint to have said that the Vice-Chancellor granted the police permission to enter the campus 'if need be and as you may deem fit'.
notes: Single secondary source read (The Quint, 20 February 2016, which calls it a 'virtual carte blanche'). The letter itself has not been seen; HuffPost India, citing NDTV, is reported in search snippets to describe it as 'purportedly' written by the Registrar, but that page could not be fetched (404 on the redirect) and is not cited as read. The Vice-Chancellor is reported in snippets to have said at a press conference that he did not invite the police; no fetched page carries that statement, so no DISPUTED record can be made yet. Obtain the letter by RTI to JNU and to the Office of the Commissioner of Police, Delhi, and the register entry for it. The Quint also reports a senior professor's claim that the Vice-Chancellor first refused and relented after the Security Officer and the Registrar stressed the gravity of the charges; that is one person's account and is not established. Quote check, 10 October 2026: The Quint page does not give the letter's date (earlier drafts said 11 February 2016) or name its addressee (earlier drafts said the Deputy Commissioner of Police, South District), so both were removed. Establish them from the letter itself.

claim: On 22 February 2016 Delhi Police were reported to be waiting outside the JNU campus for the Vice-Chancellor's permission before entering to arrest students who had returned to campus, and the teachers' association said the Vice-Chancellor had assured them the police would not enter.
notes: The Quint live blog and IANS (via ummid.com) are two reports of one situation on 22 February 2016, which is after the 12 February events. It shows police treating the university's consent as a step they sought, which is relevant context for the question of who authorised entry on 12 February, but it is a different day and not evidence about that day. The IANS report quotes the Delhi Police Commissioner, asked whether police would enter JNU, as saying he was confident his team was competent to deal with the matter and that the investigating officer would choose the best available option.

claim: Who gave the order for Delhi Police to enter the JNU campus on 12 February 2016, and who gave the order to arrest Kanhaiya Kumar, is not established by any document read for this file.
notes: No order, requisition, case-diary entry, deployment record or affidavit naming the authorising office has been found. What the documents read do show: (a) the State's account in the High Court of events up to 10 February (HIST-JNU16-003); (b) a reported Registrar's letter of 11 February about university permission (HIST-JNU16-006), which would show the university's consent and does not show who in the police or the Ministry decided to go in; (c) in Parliament, members of the Lok Sabha on 24 February 2016 criticised the Home Minister's public statements and the Commissioner's, and the Minister of Human Resource Development spoke about the permission slip and the university's own enquiry, but the record read contains no statement by the Government on who authorised the entry or the arrest (HIST-JNU16-021). Delhi Police reports to the Ministry of Home Affairs; that structure is stated in this repository's own notes, and no source fetched for this file establishes it. Routes: RTI to the Ministry of Home Affairs and to the Office of the Commissioner of Police, Delhi, for the arrest memo, the case diary, any requisition to or from JNU, and communications between the two; a question in Parliament; the Delhi High Court record of W.P.(Crl.) 558/2016, including the State's status report.

claim: The Delhi High Court (Pratibha Rani J.) granted Kanhaiya Kumar interim bail for six months on 2 March 2016 on a personal bond of Rs 10,000 and one surety, preferably a JNU faculty member, with an undertaking not to participate actively or passively in any activity which may be termed anti-national and a bar on leaving the country without the court's permission. The order records that the investigation had been transferred to the Special Cell.

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Delhi High Court order of 2 March 2016, Kanhaiya Kumar v. State (NCT of Delhi), W.P.(Crl.) 558/2016
sources.originates_from: Delhi High Court (Pratibha Rani J.); the court's own copy was not fetched

notes: The order records at paragraph 27 that 'the investigation has now been transferred to Special Cell'; it does not say which office ordered the transfer or when. The order also records the Government of NCT of Delhi's Standing Counsel supporting bail and the ASG for the State opposing it (paragraphs 18 to 25). Paragraph 56 states the observations are for deciding bail only and are not an expression on merits.

claim: On 15 February 2016, at Patiala House Courts Complex, New Delhi, people described in reports as lawyers or persons in lawyers' robes assaulted students, teachers of JNU and journalists, while the case against Kanhaiya Kumar was scheduled to be heard.

sources.originates_from: Supreme Court committee report, as quoted via LiveLaw

notes: Three outlets (The News Minute 25 February 2016; Legally India/IANS 23 July 2016; The News Minute/PTI 24 February 2016). The News Minute and Legally India draw on different wires. The Supreme Court order of 17 February 2016 itself records that 'certain unpleasant and unacceptable incidents are said to have taken place in the court premises' on 15 February (HIST-JNU16-011). Police later charged three lawyers and a Delhi BJP legislator (HIST-JNU16-016). Injury counts are not established (HIST-JNU16-012).

claim: The Supreme Court's order of 17 February 2016 in N.D. Jayaprakash v. Union of India, W.P.(Crl.) 25/2016 (Chelameswar and Sapre JJ.), records that on 15 February 2016 'a lot of people gathered including the members of the legal fraternity, students and their supporters and a large number of media persons' and that 'certain unpleasant and unacceptable incidents are said to have taken place in the court premises'. It regulated entry to the court hall for the 2 pm hearing that day: only the lawyers named for the accused, up to four family members, five named journalists, certified by the Registrar General of the Delhi High Court, with no mobile phones, and it directed the Commissioner of Police, Delhi to maintain law and order around the complex.

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Supreme Court record of proceedings, N.D. Jayaprakash v. Union of India, W.P.(Crl.) 25/2016, 17 February 2016
sources.originates_from: Supreme Court of India daily orders; the court's own copy on sci.gov.in was not fetched

notes: On 22 February 2016 the Court corrected the order on the Solicitor General's submission that on 15 February Kanhaiya Kumar 'was not in fact produced before the Patiala House Court Complex but he was only scheduled to be produced there' (see HIST-JNU16-013). The order was issued the morning of 17 February; the order states the Delhi High Court's administrative side was meeting the same day at 2 pm.

claim: The number of people injured at Patiala House Courts on 15 February 2016, and their identities and injuries, is not established by any document read for this file.
notes: No source fetched gives a count. Not found: Delhi Police FIR texts (reports say four FIRs were registered over the 15 and 17 February violence), medico-legal certificates (these need the consent of the people concerned), or the aggregate admission figures of any hospital. Routes: RTI to government hospitals for aggregate figures; the FIR copies from Delhi Police; the Delhi Police status report and chargesheets of July 2016 (Metropolitan Magistrate Snigdha Sarvaria, per Legally India).

claim: On 22 February 2016 the Supreme Court corrected its order of 17 February after the Solicitor General said that on 15 February 2016 Kanhaiya Kumar was not in fact produced before the Patiala House Courts Complex but was only scheduled to be produced there.

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Supreme Court record of proceedings, 22 February 2016
sources.originates_from: Supreme Court of India daily orders; the court's own copy was not fetched

notes: This matters for how the 15 February events are described. The reports read describe the 15 February attack as on students, teachers and journalists, and the attacks on Kanhaiya Kumar himself as on 17 February 2016 (The News Minute, PTI 24 February 2016). Some other outlets, in snippets not read as pages, put an attack on him on 15 February; the court's correction is the better record. The 22 February order also lists the reports then before the Court (HIST-JNU16-015).

claim: The Supreme Court on 17 February 2016 recorded that it deputed six members of the Bar (Kapil Sibal, Rajeev Dhawan, Dushyant Dave, H.P. Rawal, Ajit K. Sinha and A.D.N. Rao) to proceed to Patiala House Courts Complex and report the situation prevailing there, stating 'the presence of the senior advocates might help diffuse the tension'. The order calls them 'the Committee'. It records that the Court had first asked Mr Ajit K. Sinha, 'who represent the Commissioner of Police, Delhi', to obtain the Commissioner's instructions.

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Supreme Court record of proceedings, N.D. Jayaprakash v. Union of India, W.P.(Crl.) 25/2016, 17 February 2016
sources.originates_from: Supreme Court of India daily orders; the court's own copy on sci.gov.in was not fetched

notes: The Committee is a group of advocates deputed by the Court. The group is described in some reports as a 'commission'; the order does not use that word. One member, Mr Sinha, appeared for the Commissioner of Police, Delhi at the same hearing; the order and later orders show him continuing to appear for Delhi Police (for example on 22 February). Reports differ on the size of the team (one PTI report lists seven names for a six-member team); the order lists six.

claim: At about 4 pm on 17 February 2016 the Committee returned and made an oral report; the Supreme Court asked for it in writing. The order records: 'it is reported today by the members of the Committee that the accused was manhandled while he was produced before the Court today', and states 'the responsibility is exclusively is that of the Commissioner of Police, Delhi to ensure the safety of the accused'. The Commissioner of Police, through Mr Sinha, had 'personally assured the safety of the accused and all others who were permitted to attend', and the Court directed him to take necessary steps to ensure the accused's safety until he was next produced.

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Supreme Court record of proceedings, N.D. Jayaprakash v. Union of India, W.P.(Crl.) 25/2016, 17 February 2016

notes: The order records only that the accused was manhandled and does not record what the Committee said about police conduct. The office the Court addressed is the Commissioner of Police, Delhi, named by office. The order does not name the person.

claim: The written report of the Supreme Court's Committee of advocates, a pen drive of the video one member recorded on his phone, and other reports were filed in sealed cover. The order of 18 February 2016 records a report by Mr Harin P. Raval on behalf of the Committee, a report from the Delhi High Court's administration, a sealed narrative by one of the accused's counsel, and that the Delhi Police report would follow; it keeps all in sealed cover. The order of 22 February 2016 lists the reports supplied to counsel: Delhi Police's incident report dated 17 February signed by its counsel (given by the Solicitor General), the Bar Council of India's affidavit, the transcription of the video recording and Committee report given by Mr Raval, the report of the accused's counsel, a separate incident report by Mr Ajit Kumar Sinha, and the report of the Registrar General of the Delhi High Court.

The 22 February order also says the Delhi High Court's administrative committee proceedings were not supplied. The 23 February order directs the Registry to mask the Registrar General's identity in copies of the visuals and to verify the pen drive against Mr Raval's phone. Where to look: the Supreme Court registry for the sealed-cover records and any later unsealing, and the Delhi High Court Registrar General's report.

claim: Members of the Supreme Court's Committee told the Court orally on 17 February 2016 that the police did not do their job at Patiala House Courts. PTI reports Mr Dhawan saying that when the accused asked police to stop an intruder, no action was taken, that a man in dark glasses not dressed as a lawyer hit the accused and later sat in the courtroom despite a court order, and that there was a 'serious threat to the life and safety of the accused' which the police would be unable to meet.

sources.originates_from: Oral report of the committee to the Supreme Court, 17 February 2016
Supreme Court committee report, as quoted via LiveLaw

notes: These are statements by Committee members as reported, and allegations from them. The Supreme Court order of the same day records only that the accused was manhandled (HIST-JNU16-015). The News Minute quotes the written report as saying 'the atmosphere outside was surcharged and intimidating' and that there was 'an effort to create an atmosphere of fear and terror', quoted via LiveLaw, and says the report records that Mr Dhawan and Mr Sibal asked police how a person not on the Supreme Court's list could enter the courtroom without a satisfactory reply. The LiveLaw piece (27 January 2018) is an opinion article by a lawyer. The three sources all depend on the same oral and written report and are not independent of it; they are independent of one another as outlets. The 17 February events concern Kanhaiya Kumar's court appearance and are separate from the 15 February attack.

claim: Delhi Police conduct at Patiala House Courts on 15 February 2016, what officers present did or did not do and on whose instructions, is not established by any document read for this file.
notes: The Supreme Court Committee's findings, the NHRC team's findings and the Bar Council affidavit concern mainly 17 February. For 15 February the only primary document read is the Supreme Court order recording that 'unpleasant and unacceptable incidents are said to have taken place'. The Lok Sabha record of 24 February 2016 carries members' statements that police 'stood as a mute spectator' (HIST-JNU16-021), which are members' allegations. A complaint to the NHRC, reproduced in its press release, alleges police 'remained mute spectators' (HIST-JNU16-019). Not found: the Delhi Police report to the Supreme Court (due 19 February 2016), deployment orders and duty rosters for 15 February, station diary or control-room entries, or the Registrar General's report. Routes: RTI to the Office of the Commissioner of Police, Delhi and the DCP concerned; the Supreme Court record of the sealed reports; the Delhi High Court Registrar General.

claim: The National Human Rights Commission issued a notice on 17 February 2016 to the Union Home Secretary, the Chief Secretary of the Government of NCT of Delhi and the Delhi Police Commissioner on a complaint that journalists and students were beaten outside Patiala House Courts by a Delhi BJP legislator and supporters dressed as lawyers while many police officers 'remained mute spectators', and asked for an urgent report within a week.

sources.publication: National Human Rights Commission, press release of 17 February 2016

notes: VERIFIED as to what the Commission's press release says; the allegations are the complainant's and remain unproven. The reply reports are not found. LiveLaw (26 February 2016) says the NHRC report said Kumar was subjected to psychological pressure during questioning and cited serious dereliction of duty by Delhi Police for not preventing the assault or apprehending attackers; this is one secondary report of an NHRC team report, which has not been seen, and is not recorded as established. Obtain the NHRC case file and reply from the Delhi Police Commissioner.

claim: The National Human Rights Commission's press release of 19 February 2016 states that its inquiry team found that the physical assault on Kanhaiya Kumar in the Patiala House court premises on 17 February 2016 'appears to be organized and pre- planned', that what happened there 'was a major security lapse on the part of the police', and that 'there was serious dereliction of duty on the part of the police'. It also states that police were present and 'did not do anything to prevent the assault or apprehend the attackers even though they were identified by Sh. Kanhaiya Kumar then and there', and that a statement issued by police as an appeal on his behalf was 'not written by him voluntarily' and its 'content, construction and framework' were 'as dictated by the police'.

notes: Reported by LiveLaw on 26 February 2016 as part of a petition's attachments. Other outlets (India TV, Hindustan Times via PressReader) could not be read (403). The NHRC report itself has not been seen. Locate it through the NHRC case record or the petition annexures in the Supreme Court. TRACED 14 October 2026. The quotations were previously known only through LiveLaw's account of a petition's attachments. They are now read from the NHRC's own press release, which lists the team's findings. The inquiry report itself has still not been seen, and the release gives the findings as the team's, forwarded to the Commission, Delhi Police and the Director General of Prisons for comments. claim: The Lok Sabha debated 'the situation arising out of recent incidents in institutions of higher education' on 24 February 2016. The record shows members stating that police stood as 'a mute spectator' while students, teachers and journalists were attacked at Patiala House, and questioning the Home Minister's reliance on a tweet and the Commissioner's public statements; it shows the Minister of Human Resource Development describing the JNU permission slip and the university's own enquiry committee. The record read contains no statement by the Government that names who ordered the police entry onto the JNU campus on 12 February or the police presence at Patiala House on 15 February.
