The Kafila post gives the quote second-hand from an Indian Express report that was not read; PUDR paraphrases it. The Kafila author calls the statement false on the strength of video footage by a photojournalist. No finding is made here on either side.

claim: From the first days the UGC office was under heavy police presence. An AISA leader describes a 'state of near siege' on 21 and 22 October 2015. JNUSU's president told The Wire that after the students returned on 26 October the police cordoned the lane, so they sat on the pavement.

sources.publication: Kafila, guest post by the national president of AISA, 23 October 2015
The Wire, 'What Lies Behind the Occupy UGC Protest', 24 November 2015
sources.originates_from: Student and JNUSU president quotes to The Wire correspondent

notes: Both are participant accounts. No order, notification or deployment record was found for the cordon, and no document says which office directed it.

claim: On 26 October 2015 the Ministry of Human Resource Development issued an order stating that non-NET fellowships would continue for the moment and that a review committee would be formed in December. Students rejected it. On 5 November 2015 the HRD Minister, according to The Wire, issued formal orders to the UGC to scrap the decision and notified a five-member expert committee.

sources.publication: PUDR, 'Condemn Delhi Police brutality on protesting students', 2 November 2015
The Wire, 'What Lies Behind the Occupy UGC Protest', 24 November 2015
sources.originates_from: Student and JNUSU president quotes to The Wire correspondent

notes: Outcome of the policy demand only. The orders themselves were not read. The dates differ in how the two sources frame the sequence, and the HRD Minister's earlier tweet of 26 October is described by The Wire.

claim: On 9 December 2015 students marching from the UGC protest toward Parliament were stopped near Feroz Shah Road. Police used lathis, water cannon and tear gas, and detained students for several hours. The News Minute reports 150 detained, all later released, and several injured.

sources.originates_from: Quotes Deputy Commissioner of Police (New Delhi) as reported by the Indian Express; that report was not itself read

notes: Four outlets agree the force and detentions happened. The count of 150 appears only in The News Minute. Caravan puts the number of marchers at over 300 and says detainees were held at or near Parliament Street; Sabrang says three buses took students to Parliament Street police station. No source gives an injury count. Scroll reports that at the time the protest was in its 51st day. This episode is outside the date range given for the incident and is recorded because it concerns the same protest.

claim: The reasons for force on 9 December 2015 are DISPUTED. The Deputy Commissioner of Police (New Delhi) said force was used to stop a march toward Parliament, that the approved route ran from ITO via Barakhamba Road to Jantar Mantar, and that protesters turned violent and attacked police at the Le Meridien roundabout. Students and AISA's national president said the march was peaceful. Scroll describes a video it says shows no stone-pelting.

sources.originates_from: Quotes Deputy Commissioner of Police (New Delhi) as reported by the Indian Express; that report was not itself read

notes: The deputy commissioner's words (named in the secondary sources, left out here) come from the Indian Express via The News Minute and Scroll, neither of which reproduces the original. The video was not seen. A claim of groping and molestation by women protesters is an allegation by protesters only (see HIST-UGC-012).

claim: On 9 December 2015 a police officer at the cordon told Caravan's reporter, 'We have orders from above. No one from inside goes out and no one from outside gets in.' The officer wore no name badge and declined to give his name.
notes: Single source, and the reporter was himself among those detained. This shows an officer says an order existed; it does not say who issued it, what its terms were or whether it was written. No prohibitory order was found by name.

claim: Who gave the order for the October 2015 detentions near the UGC office, and for any force used on 21 to 27 October, is not established. No document read names an issuing officer or office. The only officer named in connection with October is a deputy commissioner of police (Central) who commented afterwards. The protest-side sources do not say who ordered it either.
notes: At the level of office, the candidates are the Delhi Police district whose area includes the UGC office and the police station with jurisdiction, but no page read says so and this is not asserted. Delhi Police reports to the Ministry of Home Affairs, which is the route for an RTI. Do not name any individual as the giver of an order on this record.

claim: Who gave the order for the 9 December 2015 force and detentions is not established. The deputy commissioner of police (New Delhi) publicly defended the use of force, and an unnamed officer cited 'orders from above', but no document names who authorised it.
notes: Defending a decision after the event is not evidence of who gave the order. See HIST-UGC-009 and HIST-UGC-010 for the two public statements.

claim: Whether any prohibitory order under the criminal procedure code (Section 144 of the old code, or its successor) was in force near the UGC office in October 2015 is not established. No source read mentions one for the UGC office.
notes: Several searches for a prohibitory order tied to the UGC office returned nothing. The only Section 144 result was an unrelated protest. Delhi Police issue such orders by notification; whether one existed would be shown by a Delhi Police or Delhi government notification, which was not found.

claim: PUDR wrote to the chairperson of the Delhi Commission for Women on 14 December 2015 asking for an inquiry into allegations of molestation and sexual assault by Delhi Police against women students at the 9 December 2015 march, and for action against those found responsible. It says PUDR had earlier condemned attacks on students in October 2015.

sources.publication: PUDR letter to the Delhi Commission for Women, 14 December 2015
sources.originates_from: PUDR's own letter; it proves what PUDR asked for, not that the allegations are true

notes: The letter is a complaint. The document proves what PUDR asked for; it does not prove the allegations. The letter names police personnel; those names were not checked against any record and are not repeated here. Any reply from the Commission is not known.

claim: No FIR, court petition, magisterial inquiry or human rights commission case about police conduct at the Occupy UGC protests was found in the sources read or in searches.
notes: This is an absence in what could be searched online, which is limited. Court and FIR records would be found by direct request. Not finding a case is not evidence that none exists. Conversely, no source read says police registered an FIR against protesters.

claim: Records that could be requested to answer who gave the order: Delhi Police daily diary entries for the police stations with jurisdiction over the UGC office and for Bhalswa, Kamla Market and Parliament Street stations on 21 to 27 October and 9 December 2015; deployment orders and bandobast instructions; any Section 144 notification; the detention lists and release memos for each station; the DCP (Central) and DCP (New Delhi) reports to headquarters; any Ministry of Home Affairs correspondence; and any reply by the Delhi Commission for Women to PUDR's letter.
notes: Route: RTI to the Delhi Police Public Information Officers and to the Ministry of Home Affairs, filed at each level at once, per SOURCING.md. Ten years on, retention periods may have destroyed some registers; a reply saying so is itself a record. Whether these records exist was not checked.

claim: Police cleared the Marina Beach protest camp in Chennai on the morning of 23 January 2017 using force, including batons and, in some reports, tear gas, on protesters who had gathered since mid-January against the ban on Jallikattu. The Tribune's agency report says police 'fired teargas shells and resorted to lathicharge to disperse crowds' on that day in Chennai and other cities. Police told PTI they used 'mild force' after protesters threw sand and water packets; a protester told PTI police used tear gas and batons.

sources.publication: Gulf News (PTI report; page last updated 1 November 2018)

sources.originates_from: Own reporting; says police 'forcibly evicted protesters from agitation sites across the state' on 23 January 2017

notes: Occurrence of force corroborated by three secondary outlets plus a tertiary summary. The reports are not independent of each other on detail: Gulf News carries a PTI account and the Tribune item is an agency dateline. No finding on proportionality, provocation or lawfulness. Police and protester accounts differ on whether tear gas was fired (a protester says yes, police say 'mild force'); the Tribune says tear gas shells were fired.

claim: Many of the Marina protesters were students and young people. The Tribune report records that the 'students and youth who had called the protest' say they were not involved in the violence that followed; the Wikipedia article records that on 24 January 2017 students called off their protest after talks with police and a district judge; The Federal describes most of those later charged as 'youngsters'; the one-man inquiry commission invited 'people and students' to depose. The protest was broad and not made up only of students.
notes: Included to fix the scope: this record is about a youth-led, student-heavy protest, and no source read gives a count of students among those removed or charged. Do not read it as a purely student event. Confidence is REPORTED because no source states the share of students.

claim: Injury figures for 23 January 2017 differ. Gulf News (PTI) says at least 20 people were injured in clashes with police. Wikipedia says 'around 60 people, including 33 policemen' were admitted to state-run hospitals. The Tribune says only that 'a number of policemen and members of the public were also injured'. No source read breaks the figures down into protesters and police for Marina alone, and none cites a hospital record.
notes: The figures may measure different things (Marina only against statewide, injured against admitted), so they are listed side by side. Hospital admission registers and police casualty reports would settle it.

claim: Number removed or detained on 23 January 2017 at Marina: NOT ESTABLISHED. Police told PTI about 7,000 protesters were present and about 2,000 remained in a human chain; the Tribune says 'thousands were evicted' with no arrest count. A Sri Lanka Guardian article, citing an interview with the head of the later inquiry commission, says 'more than 3,000 youths were arrested' across the protests; the interview itself was not read.

sources.originates_from: PTI, 23 January 2017; crowd estimate attributed to a police officer
Interview with Justice S. Rajeswaran in Frontline, as relayed; Frontline itself not read

notes: The 3,000 figure is relayed twice over and its date range and place are not given. It cannot be tied to Marina or to 23 January. The records that would give a count are the Chennai city police arrest and detention registers for 23 January 2017.

claim: Who gave the order to clear Marina Beach on 23 January 2017, and in what form (written or oral): NOT ESTABLISHED. No document read names an officer or office as the source of the order. Pages read that are silent on it: Tribune (23 January 2017), Gulf News/PTI, Deccan Chronicle (17 February 2017), The Federal (14 January 2021), Sri Lanka Guardian (22 January 2025), the Madras High Court judgment of 28 April 2018, and Wikipedia.
notes: Recorded at the level of office: the police operation in Chennai falls within the Greater Chennai Police, whose head is the Commissioner of Police (the office the High Court judgment records as issuing the later section 144 order). That is an inference about where the chain runs and establishes nothing about whether the Commissioner gave the order. The Chief Minister is reported by two outlets to have defended the operation in the Assembly (see HIST-C17A-009); a defence after the event is not an order. People's Watch states that the Commissioner declined to meet its fact-finding team; that is not an attribution of the order.

claim: The State told the Madras High Court, in a counter-affidavit recital recorded by Justice T. Raja at para 4 of the judgment of 28 April 2018, that 'the Commissioner of Police, Greater Chennai Police, promulgated an order under Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 on 28.1.2017 prohibiting any assembly, procession, fast, demonstration, human chain, meeting in and around Marina for a period of 15 days'. The same paragraph says the order 'also came to an end on 12.2.2017' and that it 'was rescinded on 4.2.2017'.

sources.publication: Madras High Court, P. Ayyakannu v. Government of Tamil Nadu, W.P. No. 8652 of 2018, judgment of 28 April 2018 (T. Raja J.), copy on Indian Kanoon (not the court's own site)

notes: Update 10 October 2026: the 28 April 2018 judgment this item cites was set aside by a Division Bench on 3 September 2018 (W.A. 1042 of 2018; see HIST-CRT-001). The Section 144 recital here is the State's counter-affidavit account only, and the appeal judgment does not repeat it. VERIFIED only for what the judgment records the State as saying. The order itself was not read, and the paragraph gives two end dates (rescinded 4 February; ended 12 February). The order is dated five days AFTER the 23 January operation, so it is not the authority for that operation. The paragraph also records the State's account that the January 2017 gathering involved 'anti-social elements' causing 'large scale violence and damage of public property' and that a commission under Justice S. Rajeswaran (Retd.) was then in progress. Those are the State's statements and carry no finding of the court. The fetched copy was hashed at retrieval. Under CrPC as it then stood; BNSS does not apply to 2017.

claim: Whether any prohibitory order under the Code of Criminal Procedure was in force at Marina on or before 23 January 2017, and who issued it: NOT ESTABLISHED. The only prohibitory order any document read mentions is the one of 28 January 2017 (HIST-C17A-006).
notes: The record that would answer it is the Greater Chennai Police order register and any gazette or press notice for January 2017.

claim: The National Human Rights Commission took suo motu cognisance of media reports of police action against Jallikattu protesters in Chennai and issued notices on Tuesday 24 January 2017 (date inferred from 'on Tuesday' in a report of 25 January) to the Chief Secretary, the Director General of Police and the Chennai Police Commissioner, asking for reports within two weeks. The NHRC statement as quoted says it 'has taken a serious view of the unprovoked police excesses'. That is the NHRC's stated view on media reports and reflects no finding after inquiry.
notes: Single page read. The NHRC's own release was not found. The two-week reports from the three offices, and any NHRC case number, are not public in anything read. The same report says the Tamil Nadu State Human Rights Commission invited complaints through a named Registrar (Law).

claim: The Chief Minister is reported by two outlets (Hindustan Times, Delhi edition, and Oman Daily Observer, both via PressReader) to have told the Assembly on or about 27 January 2017 that police used minimum force so that the protest would not disrupt the Republic Day function, and that action would follow against police found guilty of arson. Neither page could be opened (HTTP 403), so the wording is not confirmed.
notes: Encountered in search listings only. The primary record would be the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly proceedings for that week.

claim: A one-man Commission of Inquiry headed by a retired judge was announced in the Tamil Nadu Assembly on 31 January 2017, with terms to examine the circumstances of the violence, whether police used appropriate force, any police violations, and precautions for the future, and to report in three months. Justice S. Rajeswaran (retired, Madras High Court) began hearings on 16 February 2017. The Madras High Court judgment of 28 April 2018 records the inquiry by Justice S. Rajeswaran (Retd.) as 'under progress'.

sources.publication: Madras High Court, P. Ayyakannu v. Government of Tamil Nadu, W.P. No. 8652 of 2018, judgment of 28 April 2018 (T. Raja J.), copy on Indian Kanoon (not the court's own site)

notes: VERIFIED for the existence of the commission and its head, from the judgment. The terms of reference come from the two news items; the government order creating the commission was not read.

claim: The Rajeswaran Commission submitted its report to the Chief Minister in January 2020 after repeated extensions and questioning of 1,901 people, per a DT Next report of 20 January 2020 citing Secretariat sources. The Federal (14 January 2021) and the Sri Lanka Guardian (22 January 2025) both say it has not been published. No source read says it was tabled in the Assembly.
notes: The Federal quotes Justice Rajeswaran as saying only the government can explain why it is unpublished. DT Next said tabling was expected 'soon'; whether that happened is not established. The report is a document that could be requested from the Home Department and sought in the Assembly.

claim: The Sri Lanka Guardian reports, from an interview with Justice Rajeswaran given to Frontline, that the commission found the police actions justified, that 'undesirable elements' entered the protests, and that the report of about 950 pages clears the police of excess force. It quotes him: 'When the protesters pick up stones, the police pick up lathis.' The report itself, and the Frontline interview, were not read.

sources.originates_from: Frontline interview with Justice S. Rajeswaran, as relayed; not read

notes: Attributed to the commission head through a third-hand relay. The Federal (2021) records the same judge as saying he could not comment on the report. The article does not say who ordered the police action. These are the commission's reported conclusions, which remain unestablished, and no document read tests them.

claim: Cases arising from the January 2017 Jallikattu protests: the Tamil Nadu government issued an order on or about 20 February 2021 to withdraw 308 cases against 26,460 people (281 under investigation, 27 pending trial), excluding cases of attacks on police and damage to police vehicles; two cases carry Railways Act sections needing Union concurrence. The Chief Minister announced the move in the Assembly on 5 February 2021.
notes: The Quint item is a republication, so this is one source. The Government Order number was not given in either. The scope covers all protests in the state, Marina among them, and says nothing about which cases arose from the 23 January eviction.

claim: The Federal reports (14 January 2021) that 179 people were charged for the Madurai agitations, 64 of them at Alanganallur under IPC section 307, the rest under the Railways Act and the Tamil Nadu Property (Prevention of Damages and Loss) Act, and that the Alanganallur cases were with the CB-CID. This concerns Madurai, which is a separate place from Marina.
notes: Included because it is the only per-case count read for any location. Protesters' claim that people not directly involved were also booked is an unproven allegation reported by the outlet.

claim: People's Watch, a civil-society organisation, ran a public inquest into alleged police violence against Jallikattu protesters, based on news reports, social media, television footage and victim statements, and published an interim report. Its page says protesters turned violent on 23 January 'as police tried to forcefully disperse the crowds', and that the Chennai Police Commissioner declined to meet its fact-finding team while two named police officers did. The interim report PDF was not read.

sources.originates_from: Organisation's own summary page; interim report PDF linked but not fetched

notes: An unproven allegation by a rights organisation. Source type is secondary because it is an advocacy summary.

claim: Records that could be requested to answer who gave the order: (1) the Rajeswaran Commission report and the government order constituting it; (2) the reports the Chief Secretary, Director General of Police and Chennai Police Commissioner owed the NHRC within two weeks of 24 January 2017, and the NHRC case file; (3) Greater Chennai Police deployment orders, control-room logs and station diary entries for 22 and 23 January 2017; (4) Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly proceedings for 31 January 2017 and the days around 27 January 2017; (5) the 2021 withdrawal order; (6) the counter-affidavits in any Madras High Court petition on the eviction. A Madras High Court special mention on 23 January 2017 is reported in a search listing only; the page could not be opened.
notes: Routes follow SOURCING.md. None of these has been requested by this research. Whether a PIL on the eviction itself was filed in the Madras High Court was not established.

claim: On 21 February 2017 a seminar titled 'Cultures of Protest', organised by the English Department at Ramjas College, University of Delhi, was disrupted by ABVP supporters who objected to the invitation to JNU student Umar Khalid, and the college administration cancelled it. Newslaundry reports ABVP supporters allegedly threw bricks into the seminar room and that Khalid, advised by police stationed at the college not to attend, did not come. The Quint reports the college withdrew the invitation to Khalid and Shehla Rashid after ABVP opposed it.

sources.publication: Newslaundry, live account dated 22 February 2017 with updates to 9:27 p.m.

notes: Occurrence of the disruption and cancellation is corroborated by two outlets. Who threw what is an unproven allegation made by students and reported by Newslaundry. The Wikipedia background section (tertiary, citing The Wire) says the principal and a professor tried to reason with the protesters, that police formed a cordon to let attendees into the venue, and that a mob pelted them with stones; that text was read but is not counted as a corroborating source because it is a summary of one cited article. The Wire article was not read.

claim: On 22 February 2017 AISA students and teachers at Ramjas College set out to march to Maurice Nagar police station (no source read uses the name 'Kamla Nagar') to demand action over the previous day. Violence broke out at the college gates between ABVP supporters and the marchers and others. The Quint reports at least a dozen students and a professor of English were wounded.

sources.publication: Newslaundry, live account dated 22 February 2017 with updates to 9:27 p.m.

notes: PREMISE CHECK: the brief named the march destination as the Kamla Nagar police station. Every source read says Maurice Nagar police station, which also holds the FIR (see HIST-RAM-009). Kamla Nagar is a separate locality and no read source places the march there. The 21 February clash over the seminar invitation and the 22 February march are otherwise as described. Newslaundry says the march was planned for 1 p.m. and about 150 students from other colleges gathered outside in support.

claim: Who started the 22 February 2017 violence is disputed. AISA and affiliated teachers say ABVP members blocked entry to the college and attacked the marchers while police stood by. The Swarajya account says AISA members tried to barge into the premises after ABVP prevented the march and locked students and teachers inside. ABVP's Satender Awana said about nine ABVP members were injured, as reported by Newslaundry. Delhi Police, per IANS, described a clash between two groups, which AISA rejected.

sources.publication: Newslaundry, live account dated 22 February 2017 with updates to 9:27 p.m.

sources.originates_from: IANS wire copy; statements of Joint Commissioner Dependra Pathak and Special Commissioner S.B.K. Singh made on 23 February 2017

notes: Each version is attributed to the party that gave it. The archive makes no finding on who began the violence. Swarajya is an opinion-leaning source and is used here only to record the opposing version.

claim: Delhi Police detained students on 22 February 2017 near Maurice Nagar police station. Newslaundry reports students demanding an FIR were 'picked by Delhi Police' and 'carried to an unknown location in a bus' and that, in its 9:27 p.m. update, 'the 100-odd students who were picked up by Delhi Police have been released near Hauz Khas'. Swarajya says there was 'a crackdown by the Police, followed by detention of the agitating students'. CPJ reports police pushed ABVP members onto a police bus and held students arrested in the fighting at Maurice Nagar police station.

sources.publication: Newslaundry, live account dated 22 February 2017 with updates to 9:27 p.m.

notes: That detentions happened is corroborated. The count is not: only Newslaundry gives a figure (about 100, in narration) and the sources differ on whether those held were AISA-side marchers, ABVP members or both. See HIST-RAM-005. No source read says whether the detentions were under a statutory power, were recorded in a detention memo, or who authorised them.

claim: Number and identity of people detained on 22 February 2017: Newslaundry says about 100 students who had gathered outside Maurice Nagar police station were picked up and released near Hauz Khas. CPJ says ABVP members were also detained and put on a police bus. DUSU president Amit Tanwar, as reported by Newslaundry, said 'no ABVP member is on the bus that's picked up protestors'. A PTI quote from an unnamed senior police official giving 40 to 50 detained 'to prevent further escalation' was seen only in a search-result summary and was not read.

sources.publication: Newslaundry, live account dated 22 February 2017 with updates to 9:27 p.m.

notes: Conflict is between the DUSU president's statement and CPJ's account about who was on the bus, and between about 100 (Newslaundry) and a possible 40 to 50 (unread PTI line, not relied on). The unread PTI figure is NOT a source for this record. No official detention list was found. A Business World page said to carry the PTI line returned HTTP 403 and was not read.

claim: Injury counts for 21 and 22 February 2017 differ by source. AISA said more than 20 teachers and students were badly injured and treated at hospitals including Hindu Rao (as reported by Newslaundry). The Quint reports at least a dozen students and a professor of English wounded. Professor Prashanto Chakrabarty was reported admitted to Hindu Rao Hospital. Delhi Police officials said a few policemen, including the SHO of Maurice Nagar police station, were roughed up (PTI via The Tribune). Swarajya, citing The Indian Express, gives eight police personnel including an SHO. ABVP said about nine of its members were injured.

sources.publication: Newslaundry, live account dated 22 February 2017 with updates to 9:27 p.m.

notes: Counts are the claims of AISA, ABVP, police and press and none comes from medical-legal records. No MLC or hospital record was read. The Indian Express article behind the 'eight police personnel' figure was not read; it is relayed by Swarajya.

claim: Journalists were assaulted on 22 February 2017. CPJ reports The Quint's Taruni Kumar was attacked around 1 p.m. while filming detentions (by a woman, not by police, according to the article) and that police attacked at least two Quint journalists, Anant Prakash and Shiv Kumar Maurya, outside the police station that evening; Prakash is quoted: 'We told them repeatedly that we are from the media, and they said, "Then you should get beaten up even more".' Newslaundry names further journalists it says were attacked. The NHRC notice cited complaints that police took cameras from media persons and that journalists were slapped, punched and kicked.

sources.publication: Newslaundry, live account dated 22 February 2017 with updates to 9:27 p.m.

notes: These are allegations, attributed to the journalists and to complaints reported by Governance Now. CPJ names no police officer. The Delhi Union of Journalists, per IANS, noted some officers wore no nametags (see HIST-RAM-010 sources).

claim: WHO GAVE THE ORDER for the detentions of 22 February 2017: NOT ESTABLISHED. No document read names the person or office that ordered the students to be picked up, put on a bus and released near Hauz Khas. The only police explanation seen in any form (an unnamed senior official telling PTI the detentions were to prevent escalation) was not read and is not relied on.

sources.publication: Newslaundry, live account dated 22 February 2017 with updates to 9:27 p.m.

notes: Newslaundry, CPJ and Swarajya say detentions occurred and name no officer or order. No detention memo, daily diary entry, DCP North or Special Commissioner order, or magistrate record was found.

claim: Special Commissioner of Police (Law and Order) S.B.K. Singh, speaking to students protesting at Delhi Police headquarters on 23 February 2017, was asked why police lathi-charged students at the Maurice Nagar protest and said: 'I did not order it. I can't tell you the name of the person who did.' IANS separately reports he said he did not know who ordered the baton charge and promised a Crime Branch probe. Singh is also reported to have said that only one FIR was filed and that it named no individual: 'As both sides received injuries, we registered the FIR.'

sources.originates_from: IANS wire copy; statements of Joint Commissioner Dependra Pathak and Special Commissioner S.B.K. Singh made on 23 February 2017

notes: This establishes only what an officer said on the record to students and the press. It is a statement by an office-holder that he did not give the order and could not name who did. It has no standing as an order or as an inquiry finding. The Asian Age quote and the IANS paraphrase come from the same event but different reporters; the Oman Observer and Peninsula pieces are the same IANS wire. claim: On 11 April 2017 police used force against Panjab University students at the Sector 14 campus in Chandigarh during a shutdown called against a 12.5 per cent fee hike: Newslaundry reports water cannon, tear gas shells and sticks; Zee News reports a clash with police; Democracy Now says officers attacked students with water cannon, batons and tear gas; a participant writing on Kafila describes a lathi charge and chasing into hostels.

Kafila (opinion piece) says at least 66 students were charged with sedition and that the complainant asked for it to be dropped. Zee News reports the university asked police in writing on 12 April 2017 to drop it, the Chief Security Officer writing that the slogans were aimed at the University Grants Commission and the Human Resource Development Ministry and were 'not against the state'. Whether the cases were in fact withdrawn is not established.
notes: Two outlets, each for a separate statement, so this is REPORTED and not corroborated for any single fact. The court production record, bail orders and any withdrawal application are the records to seek. No Punjab and Haryana High Court order on the case was found.

claim: Records that could be requested to answer who gave the order: (1) the FIR registered over the 11 April 2017 events, and the university's complaint and letter asking for the sedition charge to be dropped; (2) Chandigarh Police deployment orders, control-room logs and station diary entries for 6, 10 and 11 April 2017; (3) the custody register of the Sector 11 and Sector 24 police stations; (4) any communication from the Vice Chancellor's office or the university's Chief Security Officer to police requesting presence on campus; (5) court production and bail records; (6) the Senate and core committee minutes (26 March and 7 May 2017 meetings are named in the sources read); (7) the Rajya Sabha reply; (8) hospital records for the roughly 50 injured, with consent.
notes: None requested by this research. The university is a public authority and the police are a public authority for RTI purposes, but no filing route or office designation for Chandigarh was established here, and none is borrowed from another jurisdiction.

claim: Union Home Minister Amit Shah said on 30 January 2020 that he spoke to the Delhi Police Commissioner and directed him to take 'strictest action'. The case was reported to have been transferred to the Delhi Police Crime Branch.

claim: Retired police officials quoted by Scroll.in on 31 January 2020 criticised the police response, and one said he did not know what instructions the personnel had. Not resolved here. The Quint (28 January) says protests reached 12 districts in two days and that around 400 students were allegedly provoked at Rajendra Nagar, per the FIR. Whether the 24 January blockade began as the district administration's release describes (afternoon, Rajendra Nagar Terminal) is taken from that release as quoted by PTI.

claim: On 24 January 2022 police used force to clear the track at Rajendra Nagar Terminal, Patna. The Patna district administration's release, as quoted by PTI, described the force as 'mild' and said it was used after officials had failed to pacify the protesters. ETV Bharat (25 January) reports police fired tear gas shells and used a water cannon; ETV Bharat (29 January) says Patna Police 'had to use batons'; ETV Bharat Hindi (26 January) refers to a lathi charge.

sources.originates_from: Patna district administration release of 24 or 25 January 2022, as quoted
Patna district administration release and East Central Railway statement, as quoted by PTI

notes: The use of force is acknowledged by the district administration itself. Its extent is DISPUTED in the sense that the administration says 'mild' while the outlets name tear gas, a water cannon and lathis; see HIST-RRB-003. The sources share an upstream (the administration release and agency copy), so they are not fully independent of one another.

claim: The extent of force used on students at Rajendra Nagar Terminal on 24 January 2022 is DISPUTED. Version 1 (Patna district administration release, via PTI): 'mild' use of force after attempts by officials to pacify the protesters failed. Version 2 (ETV Bharat, 25 January 2022): tear gas shells and a water cannon were used. Version 3 (ETV Bharat Hindi, 26 January 2022): police 'rained lathis' on students; a lathi charge at the terminal is said to have spread the protest to other districts.

notes: No injury count from any official source was found. No medical or hospital record was found. The two versions are not necessarily exclusive: 'mild' is the administration's word and the others describe the instruments.

claim: The number of people injured by police action in Patna in January 2022 is not established. No official count and no hospital figure was found in the sources read.
notes: Search turned up one snippet claiming more than two dozen students were hospitalised in Patna, with unclear attribution. The page was not fetched and is not cited. A request to the Patna district hospitals for aggregate admissions for 24 to 28 January 2022 is the route.

claim: At least four people were arrested after the Rajendra Nagar Terminal protest of 24 January 2022. The Patna District Magistrate said on 27 January 2022 that four people had been arrested for stone pelting and vandalism at the terminal.

claim: The Quint (28 January 2022), citing The Indian Express and ANI, reports that Patna Police had arrested eight students. The article does not say which of the sixteen students named in the FIR were the eight.

sources.publication: The Quint, 28 January 2022 (cites The Indian Express and ANI)

sources.publication: The Quint, 28 January 2022 (cites The Indian Express and ANI)

See HIST-RRB-008. These are allegations in a police complaint. Nothing here is a finding against any named person. Sections are as printed by The Quint and have not been checked against the FIR.

The Patna DM said on 27 January that six coaching teachers 'were named for provoking' the students by those arrested during the enquiry. claim: A Patna district administration release, as quoted by PTI on 25 January 2022, said it was 'suspected that the protesters might have been instigated by those running coaching institutes for competitive exams' and that 'all those found complicit will face action'.

Patna district administration release and East Central Railway statement, as quoted by PTI

claim: Who ordered or authorised the use of force at Rajendra Nagar Terminal on 24 January 2022 is not established by any document read. The only account found is the district administration's own release, as quoted by PTI, which says force was used after attempts by officials led by the District Magistrate and the Senior Superintendent of Police to pacify the protesters had failed. That places the decision with the district administration and district police at the scene. No order, deployment record, control-room log or magisterial inquiry was found.

sources.originates_from: Patna district administration release of 24 or 25 January 2022, as quoted
Patna district administration release and East Central Railway statement, as quoted by PTI

Records that could settle it: deployment orders and station diary of the Patna railway police and district police for 24 January 2022, and any magisterial inquiry order.

claim: Police entry into student lodges, hostels or coaching hostels in Patna during the January 2022 railway-exam protests is not established. No source read reports it for Patna.

claim: The Ministry of Railways issued a notice on 25 January 2022 warning that candidates 'found indulging in unlawful activities' during the NTPC protests would be 'liable to both police action as well as lifetime debarment from a Railway job' and that protest videos would be examined with the help of specialised agencies. On 26 January 2022 it suspended the NTPC and Level 1 exams and announced a committee to examine candidates' grievances.

This is a Union ministry statement of consequences. It is not an order to any state police force, and no source links it to the Patna or Prayagraj operations. The committee date for recommendations is given as 4 March 2022 by The Quint.

claim: On 26 January 2022 protesting aspirants set a train coach on fire at Gaya. ETV Bharat Hindi (26 January) also reports that a rail engine was set on fire at Nawada station, without giving its date. claim: The Indian Youth Congress said on 27 January 2022 that it had filed a complaint with the National Human Rights Commission alleging violation of the human rights of students at the hands of the police forces of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, and asking that the DGPs of both states be directed to act against the concerned superintendents of police.

sources.originates_from: Indian Youth Congress statement of 27 January 2022

notes: This records that a complaint was filed, as stated by the complainant. No NHRC registration number, notice, report call or outcome was found. Do not treat it as NHRC action. The NHRC case status can be requested or searched by diary number if the Indian Youth Congress will share it.

claim: No Patna High Court proceeding, no NHRC or Bihar State Human Rights Commission action, no judicial or magisterial inquiry, and no suspension of any Bihar police officer connected to the January 2022 railway-exam protests was found. The outcome of the Patrakar Nagar FIR (arrests of the named teachers, bail, charge sheet, quashing or withdrawal) was not found.
notes: Absence in the sources searched is not evidence that none exists. Searches in English and Hindi for a Patna High Court matter returned only unrelated 2026 matters involving the same lead teacher. Routes: eCourts search in Patna civil and sessions court, Patna High Court case status, RTI to Patna SSP office, and to the Bihar home department for any inquiry.

claim: On 25 January 2022 in Prayagraj, aspirants protesting the RRB NTPC results sat on the railway line near the station area; police dispersed them, and police entered nearby student lodges and used lathis on students. Videos of police breaking doors and beating students circulated and led to suspensions.

sources.originates_from: Statements of the Prayagraj SSP at Police Lines, Prayagraj, 26 January 2022, as reported

notes: Five outlets, with Newslaundry reporting from lodges in Chota Baghara weeks later and Alt News using the same account (its main point is a mis-dated photo used by another paper, which it removes from the evidence). Date: the incident is 25 January 2022 (Tuesday). Deccan Herald (26 January) and India TV give the same day. The BW piece gives the location as Chota Baghada. Police wording is in HIST-RRB-019.

claim: How the victims are described in the sources: Deccan Herald says 'several students' on the tracks were injured, 'some seriously', and that videos showed police forcing students out of rooms in inns and guesthouses and hitting them. Newslaundry describes residents of two lodges, mostly students living in single rooms, who told it police 'stormed inside and began beating everyone with lathis'; one resident said he had sat the NTPC exam but 'had nothing to do with protests' and was hit; another said students were treated 'in a similar way' to how terrorists are weeded out. These are interviews that make no findings.
notes: Individuals are not named here. Newslaundry also reports that many students left their rooms out of fear. No injury count, no hospital figure and no count of people detained inside lodges was found. Alt News flags one widely used injury photo as a 2019 image from elsewhere, so unverified injury photographs from 28 January coverage should not be used.

claim: Police account of why they entered the lodges is DISPUTED. Version 1 (Prayagraj SSP, as reported by PTI/India TV on 27 January 2022): some of the protesters pelted police with stones and hid in a nearby hostel; police were trying to catch them; some personnel used unnecessary force, which was visible in the video. Version 2 (residents interviewed by Newslaundry, 10 February 2022): police entered rooms and beat everyone, including people who had not been at the protest. Version 3 (Alt News, 29 January 2022): students were chased from the tracks, some allegedly pelted stones, and police then forcibly entered a hostel and lathi-charged students.

sources.originates_from: Statements of the Prayagraj SSP at Police Lines, Prayagraj, 26 January 2022, as reported

notes: Version 3 is Alt News's summary and partly agrees with each of the others. What was thrown, by whom, and who among those beaten had taken part, is not established by any document.

claim: The Prayagraj SSP said at Police Lines on 26 January 2022 that a video had surfaced in which some policemen were seen using unnecessary force, that the policemen shown had been identified, suspended with immediate effect and made subject to departmental action. The number suspended is DISPUTED. Version 1 (Deccan Herald, 26 January 2022, 'officials'): three. Version 2 (PTI via India TV and Oneindia, 27 January 2022; ANI via The Quint; Newslaundry, 10 February 2022; Alt News, 29 January 2022): six, listed by PTI as one officer without a stated rank, two sub-inspectors and three constables.

sources.originates_from: Statements of the Prayagraj SSP at Police Lines, Prayagraj, 26 January 2022, as reported
Statements of the Prayagraj SSP, as reported by PTI
Ministry of Railways notices of 25 and 26 January 2022, as quoted; statements of SSP Gaya and SSP Prayagraj to ANI

Officers are not named here; the SSP's statement names them as reported by PTI and no suspension order was read. Whether departmental action ended in any punishment was not found. Newslaundry (10 February) states six were suspended.

claim: Who gave the order for the dispersal and for entry into lodges in Prayagraj on 25 January 2022 is not established. The only on-record position found is the Prayagraj SSP's: that some personnel used unnecessary force, which was visible in the video, and were suspended. That describes the force used by the suspended personnel as unnecessary and does not say what order they were acting on. No deployment order, control-room log, inquiry report or statement by the Uttar Pradesh DGP or state home department was found.

An 11-member police team was set up, per the SSP, to investigate the alleged funding of the protest (see HIST-RRB-022). Whether an inquiry into police conduct was held and who led it was not found: Deccan Herald (26 January) says one 'would be conducted'.

The Prayagraj SSP said it was against about 1,000 unidentified people under 13 serious sections, for rioting and blocking the track. Deccan Herald (26 January) says 1,500 students. The SSP also said two people had been arrested and an 11-member team was formed after he said it appeared the accused took 'money from some political parties' to create unrest. That is the SSP's allegation, as reported by PTI. No evidence for it appears in any source read.

claim: A local activist who convenes a student platform in Prayagraj told Newslaundry (10 February 2022) that he was named as main accused in the FIR over the protest and spent five days in jail. The activist said he had sent video of the lodge violence to the NHRC and thought that may have counted against him with police.

claim: No court order, NHRC registration, state human rights commission action or inquiry report concerning the Prayagraj police action of 25 January 2022 was found. The Indian Youth Congress complaint to the NHRC (HIST-RRB-015) is the only oversight-body step in the sources.

Routes: NHRC online case search, Allahabad High Court case status, RTI to the Prayagraj Police Commissionerate or SSP office for the suspension orders, the inquiry order and its report, and the FIR; RTI to the UP Home (Police) department.

claim: On 17 June 2022 a protest by army recruitment aspirants against the Agnipath scheme at Secunderabad railway station, Telangana, turned violent (a train was set on fire and station property damaged). Security personnel fired at the crowd and one man, Damera Rakesh, died of a bullet injury.

sources.publication: The Tribune (PTI copy), dateline Hyderabad 17 June 2022, updated 18 June 2022

notes: Occurrence corroborated by several outlets. The Tribune copy is PTI; the others are separate reports. Cause of death is as reported, from hospital staff quoted by the press; no post-mortem report was read. Who fired is DISPUTED, see HIST-AGN-002. The victim is described in every report as an army job aspirant (some say he had cleared the medical test and was awaiting the written exam). No source read here calls him a student. Interpretation of the scope note: he qualifies as a person who faced violence.

claim: Reports conflict on which force fired at Secunderabad. Version A: the Railway Protection Force (RPF) fired, per 'a senior police official' quoted by PTI, per Siasat, and per Careers360 which attributes to the GRP the statement that RPF personnel 'opened fire on the mob preventing them from setting fire to the loco engines'. Version B: Deccan Chronicle writes 'Officials confirmed that the RPF was never given any orders to shoot and that it was the state police who fired at the mob with rubber bullets', and reports about 10 rounds. Version C: ThePrint says Telangana Police 'resorted to aerial firing'. The Hans India says 'Railway Police opened fire'.

sources.publication: The Tribune (PTI copy), dateline Hyderabad 17 June 2022, updated 18 June 2022

notes: All officials in these reports are unnamed, except Railway SP B. Anuradha, who is quoted on cases booked only. Reports also differ on ammunition (rubber bullets, aerial firing, bullet injuries reported by the hospital). No source read here gives a ballistic or post-mortem finding. Tribune and Careers360 may share PTI origin. A tweet or statement attributing the firing to state police by a political figure was seen only in a search snippet and is not recorded.

claim: Unnamed officials described the decision to fire as collective or as taken on higher instructions. Careers360 quotes an unnamed South Central Railway official saying the decision to open fire was taken collectively ('decisions are collective in such situations'). Siasat writes that 'on instructions of the higher' ups the policemen fired on the mob; it names no official. Siasat also reports an unnamed senior police official held talks with protesters before the final action, and Deccan Chronicle names Sandeep Shandiliya (Director General, Rail and Road Safety) and A.R. Srinivas (additional commissioner of crimes) as holding talks with protesters, without saying either gave a firing order.
notes: These are attributed press accounts from unnamed officials. They place the decision at the level of 'higher' offices in the railway police and/or state police without identifying the office. Do not read the two named officers as having given any order: the source says only that they held talks.

claim: The individual or office that gave the order to fire at Secunderabad on 17 June 2022 is not established by any document read for this record. No police statement, inquiry report, affidavit or court order naming the person or office was found.
notes: Searched for statements by the GRP, RPF, Hyderabad police and Telangana DGP, and for a magisterial inquiry, Telangana High Court or NHRC proceeding. Nothing found. A protester quoted by Deccan Chronicle asked 'who gave orders to open fire on us' (reported, unanswered). Absence from search results is not proof no such document exists.

claim: Injury and victim details differ across reports. Injured protesters: 12 (Siasat, The Quint), 13 (Careers360, Hans India), 14 (Deccan Chronicle headline; its text gives 2 surgery cases plus 11 minor). Two protesters had surgery (chest injury; fractured femur) per The Quint and Deccan Chronicle. The Quint adds seven police personnel injured; Careers360 and ThePrint say police personnel were injured without a count. Victim age: 18 (Deccan Chronicle), 21 (Sakshi Post), 22 (Hans India, Siasat lead), 24 (Tribune, The Quint, Siasat body).

sources.publication: The Tribune (PTI copy), dateline Hyderabad 17 June 2022, updated 18 June 2022

Victim: Damera Rakesh of Dabeerpet village, Khanapur mandal, Warangal district, described by The Quint and Tribune as an army aspirant, son of a farmer. Name spelled Damera, Damira and Damodar Rakesh in different reports.

claim: The Government Railway Police (GRP), Secunderabad, registered a case against the protesters after the 17 June 2022 violence. SP B. Anuradha is quoted: 'We booked cases against them.'
notes: FIR number, police station and complainant were not found. This record concerns the case against protesters. No source read reports an FIR or case about the firing or the death.

claim: ThePrint reports the railway police case cites Indian Penal Code sections 143, 147, 324, 307, 435, 427, 448, 336, 332 and 341.
notes: Single source, no FIR copy read. Section list not checked against the FIR.

claim: Arrests: Deccan Chronicle (18 June 2022) reports that officials said police detained 26 individuals. The Hans India (25 June 2022) reports 55 persons arrested and eight others being sought, and that GRP reportedly arrested Avula Subba Rao, director of Sai Defence Academy, whom police describe as the prime suspect, along with associates named only as Shiva and Hari. The Hans India (24 June 2022) reports Telangana Congress chief A. Revanth Reddy saying 50 of the 55 arrested are Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe and that they were jailed under sections 'usually invoked against terrorists'.

Revanth Reddy's statement is a political allegation and is attributed to him. The Hans India says police 'will announce his arrest soon', so the arrest was not formally confirmed in that article. Court custody details were not found in a page read.

claim: The News Minute (19 June 2022) reports that the Telangana State Human Rights Commission asked the RPF and GRP for a report, with 20 July given as the deadline.
notes: Single source, and the commission's own order was not found or read. This is the state commission, a body separate from the NHRC. No NHRC action, Telangana High Court petition or magisterial inquiry was found. The report's contents and the commission's outcome are unknown.

claim: Telangana Chief Minister K. Chandrasekhar Rao announced Rs 25 lakh ex gratia and a government job for a family member of Damera Rakesh on 17 June 2022. A Government Order issued on 24 June 2022 directed compassionate appointment of his elder brother, Damera Ram Raju, and told the Warangal district Collector to act.
notes: The Government Order itself was not read; the account is from press. The Chief Minister is also quoted by Careers360 as blaming the Centre's 'faulty procedures' for the death. That is a political statement with no standing as a finding.

claim: Whether any magisterial inquiry, judicial inquiry, NHRC case, Telangana High Court petition, or prosecution or departmental action over the firing exists is not established.
notes: Searches for these returned nothing relating to this incident. Treat as a gap to fill by RTI and eCourts search. The gap leaves open whether any exists.

claim: On 20 September 2018 a protest by students and parents against the posting of Urdu and Sanskrit teachers at Darivit High School, Islampur block, Uttar Dinajpur district, West Bengal, ended in a confrontation with police in which two young men, Tapas Barman and Rajesh Sarkar, died of gunshot injuries. The Calcutta High Court judgment of 10 May 2023 records the event as the subject of FIR No. 611 of 2018 (paras 1 to 4) and orders compensation to the families of those 'killed and injured' (para 77). The court does not find who fired the shots.

sources.publication: Calcutta High Court judgment of 10 May 2023 (Justice Rajasekhar Mantha) in WPA 20733, 20734 and 20938 of 2018, Nilkamal Sarkar, Badal Barman and Subhash Sarkar v. State of West Bengal, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)
The Indian Express (Express News Service), 20 September 2018

notes: The two deaths are named in the judgment (paras 4, 12), which is the document this archive relies on for the names. Ages differ: Indian Express and Hindustan Times (2018) give 19 and 21 for the two. The judgment calls the dead 'boys' and 'students' in the NHRC extract and does not give ages. Whether either was a minor is not established here. Both are described by the press as former students of the school. Indian Express (20 September 2018) first reported one death; the second death was reported the next day (HT, 23 September 2018: one died 'on the spot', the other 'on Friday').

claim: Police used tear gas and rubber bullets at Darivit High School on 20 September 2018. This is stated by the police themselves: the High Court records the gist of the police FIR as saying 'The police too fired tear gas and rubber bullets' (para 4), and the Superintendent of Police of the district was quoted on the day saying 'We have fired rubber bullets and tear gas shells. We did not fire bullets.'

sources.publication: Calcutta High Court judgment of 10 May 2023 (Justice Rajasekhar Mantha) in WPA 20733, 20734 and 20938 of 2018, Nilkamal Sarkar, Badal Barman and Subhash Sarkar v. State of West Bengal, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)
The Indian Express (Express News Service), 20 September 2018

notes: The SP's quotation is from The Indian Express, 20 September 2018, and is a newspaper's report of a spoken statement. The FIR account is a primary document as recited by the court (the FIR itself was not read). The same sources attribute the first use of force to a mob attacking the police. That attribution is the police version and is not found by the court.

claim: Whether police use of force on 20 September 2018 was excessive, and what it included, is DISPUTED. (a) Police and State version: police were 'suddenly attacked by an unruly mob with bricks, lathi, bombs, and firearms' (FIR gist, para 4) and the CID report is 'the actual sequence of events' (State counsel, para 28). (b) NHRC version, quoted in the judgment (para 25, conclusion iii): 'The police action seems to have used excessive force (lathi charge, tear gas, rubber bullets) without any warning and landed up beating students, misbehavior with girl students'. The State argued that no complainant or petitioner alleged molestation of girl students and that the complainants did not come forward to depose (para 42). The court did not make its own finding on molestation; it accepted the NHRC report only 'as a preliminary inquiry finding' (para 58) and listed among the NHRC findings that police 'may have used excessive force to break through the students and enter the school' (para 59(c)). Indian Express (20 September 2018) reported that police resorted to lathi charge 'as the students lobbed bricks and stones'.

sources.publication: Calcutta High Court judgment of 10 May 2023 (Justice Rajasekhar Mantha) in WPA 20733, 20734 and 20938 of 2018, Nilkamal Sarkar, Badal Barman and Subhash Sarkar v. State of West Bengal, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)
The Indian Express (Express News Service), 20 September 2018

notes: No finding of guilt or intent is made here. The NHRC report itself was not read; only the extracts quoted in the judgment. The judgment says the NHRC report 'may be without jurisdiction and cannot technically or legally be called a statutory report' (para 47) because the State Human Rights Commission had taken cognisance first, and the State asked the court to ignore it entirely (para 29).

claim: Who fired the bullets that killed two men is DISPUTED. (a) Police and State: police deny firing bullets (SP quoted in Indian Express, 20 September 2018, and Hindustan Times, 23 September 2018); the State told the court 'The police were not responsible for the firing' (para 28); the FIR names bullet injuries as caused in an attack on police by a mob with firearms (para 4); the CID theory is that a person in the mob fired. The Chief Minister said police did not open fire (NDTV, 23 September 2018). (b) Families and the NHRC: the NHRC conclusion quoted at para 25 says villagers 'unambiguously alleged that the last police vehicle had fired', and that the autopsy analysis was 'suggestive of use of rifled weapon fired from a short range and may be from a slight height (may be aboard a vehicle as alleged)'. (c) The court: it found the CID theory that a person in the mob fired 'incredible' (para 61(f)) and recorded 'a strong possibility that bullets had been fired from the last police vehicle leaving the place of occurrence' as a point drawn from one injured person's statement to the NHRC (para 61(h)). It also records that the State told the court the CID 'could not arrive at any conclusion as regards the firing of the bullets and the weapon used therefor' (para 41).

sources.publication: Calcutta High Court judgment of 10 May 2023 (Justice Rajasekhar Mantha) in WPA 20733, 20734 and 20938 of 2018, Nilkamal Sarkar, Badal Barman and Subhash Sarkar v. State of West Bengal, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)
The Indian Express (Express News Service), 20 September 2018

notes: The court's statements are made in deciding to transfer the investigation and are described by the court as reasons to doubt the CID's work, not as a trial finding on who fired. Nobody has been convicted or charged on the court's reading in the documents read. The weapon, and who held it, are not established in any document read.

claim: Who gave the order for police to go to Darivit High School, to enter or break through to the school gate, and to use lathis, tear gas and rubber bullets: NOT ESTABLISHED. No document read names the person or the office that gave any of these orders. The judgment records the FIR account that police received information at 2.05 pm (GD entry No. 875), that the Inspector-in-Charge of Islampur police station, with a contingent of additional officers and police force, reached the school (para 3), and the NHRC's extract that the police 'were ill equipped' at first and that 'Reinforcements were later called by the police' (para 25, iii) without saying who called them.

sources.publication: Calcutta High Court judgment of 10 May 2023 (Justice Rajasekhar Mantha) in WPA 20733, 20734 and 20938 of 2018, Nilkamal Sarkar, Badal Barman and Subhash Sarkar v. State of West Bengal, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)

notes: Level of office: the only rank the judgment places at the scene is the Inspector-in-Charge of the police station, as the FIR's own account. Whether the Sub-Divisional Police Officer, the Superintendent of Police or the District Magistrate was present or gave any direction is not stated in any document read. The Indian Express (20 September 2018) quotes the District Magistrate as saying he was 'waiting for the police report' and the SP as saying police 'have fired rubber bullets and tear gas shells', and says nothing about who ordered either. Documents that could settle it are listed at HIST-DAR-014 and HIST-DAR-015.

claim: Who gave the order to fire live ammunition, if police did so: NOT ESTABLISHED. Police deny that any live firing by police took place. The High Court says in a passage on the CID's failings that the CID 'may have had serious inhibitions in having to investigate any conspiracy angle that may have led to blaming any police officials for having fired any weapon, or any higher police official ordering such firing into a mob without provocation, at the instance of any person or persons in power' (para 71). The court states this as a possibility about the CID's inhibitions and makes no finding that any such order was given.

sources.publication: Calcutta High Court judgment of 10 May 2023 (Justice Rajasekhar Mantha) in WPA 20733, 20734 and 20938 of 2018, Nilkamal Sarkar, Badal Barman and Subhash Sarkar v. State of West Bengal, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)

notes: Quoted because it is the one passage in a primary document that raises the question of an order to fire. It names no officer, office or political figure as having given one. Para 19(h) records the petitioners' submission that only the CBI 'can investigate the role of influential political persons in the incident and the role of the State police in the death of the two boys'; that is the petitioners' submission.

claim: On 23 September 2018 the father of one of the dead men made a complaint that named four people as responsible for the incident: Sumit Kumar, Superintendent of Police, Uttar Dinajpur; Rajen Chettri, Inspector-in-Charge, Islampur; Golam Rabbani, MLA, Islampur constituency; and Kanailal Agarwal, Chairman, Islampur Municipality (judgment para 7). Whether the complaint was received is DISPUTED. The petitioner says the Islampur police station refused to register it and then emailed it to the Chief Secretary (para 7). The State told the court it 'was never sent to or received by either the Islampur P.S. or the CID' (para 27). The court noted that the State had not denied the refusal in its affidavit in opposition and had admitted knowledge of it (para 62(e)), and that the complaint had been annexed to the writ petition filed on 4 October 2018, so it could not be said to have been unknown to the CID (para 62(c)).

sources.publication: Calcutta High Court judgment of 10 May 2023 (Justice Rajasekhar Mantha) in WPA 20733, 20734 and 20938 of 2018, Nilkamal Sarkar, Badal Barman and Subhash Sarkar v. State of West Bengal, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)

notes: The complaint names these people as responsible for the incident. The judgment does not say the complaint alleges any of them gave an order, and the court makes no finding against any of them. Names appear here only because the judgment records them and this record quotes it. The complaint also appears in the judgment as dated both 23 September 2018 (paras 7, 62) and 25 September 2018 (para 19(a)); the two dates are the court's own inconsistency. A separate complaint by the father of the other dead man, dated 21 September 2018, is recorded at para 8.

claim: On 18 November 2019, the first day of the Winter Session of Parliament, students of Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) marched from the campus towards Parliament against a hostel fee hike and were stopped by Delhi Police before reaching it, with detentions. NDTV quotes a former students' union president saying the march was stopped about a kilometre from Parliament's north gate.

claim: On 19 November 2019 opposition members raised the police action against JNU students in Parliament. The Deccan Herald reports that Rajya Sabha proceedings were adjourned in the first half of the day after Left party members sought discussion, and that Congress and BSP members in the Lok Sabha Zero Hour demanded 'a high-level probe'. No government reply on the police action was found.
notes: A Zero Hour mention is not a written answer. A search for a Home Ministry written answer on the 18 November march in the 2019 Winter Session returned none; the sansad.in question archive was not itself searched, so absence is not established. Lead for a legislature route: ask a member to table a question to the Ministry of Home Affairs on who authorised the deployment and Section 144.

claim: Delhi Police inquiry into the lathicharge allegations of 18 November 2019: the Newslaundry reporter's diary quotes a post by the Delhi Police PRO, via ANI, saying police would 'inquire into lathi charge allegations'. No page read reports that an inquiry was opened, who headed it, or its result.

sources.originates_from: Post by Delhi Police PRO on social media, quoted by Newslaundry

notes: The social media post was not itself retrieved. Outcome unknown. This is a single secondary relay of a police statement.

claim: On 9 December 2019 JNU students marched from the campus towards Rashtrapati Bhavan to petition the President over the hostel fee hike. Reports that police lathi-charged them: The Hindu reports two lathicharges (one at the Africa Avenue and Ring Road crossing when some students tried to turn right towards AIIMS, a second of 'several minutes' after the students' union president began addressing students from a police vehicle); Newslaundry reports lathicharges near Bhikaji Cama Place and about 5 pm; NewsMobile, Gulf News and The Tribune report a lathicharge after students tried to cross barricades. Onmanorama reports that police 'refuted the charges of lathicharge and detention of students'.

Onmanorama (page carries a December 2020 stamp that conflicts with its URL date of 9 December 2019)

We don't want to beat them up but we are left with no choice.' A DCP is quoted there as saying students 'are being dropped back at the campus'. The Hindu says the march left campus at 2 pm escorted by police and paramilitary personnel.

claim: Detentions on 9 December 2019: the students' union president said 'Several students, including women, have been detained by police' (The Tribune). Onmanorama (page carries a December 2020 stamp that conflicts with its URL date of 9 December 2019)

sources.publication: The Tribune (Tribune Web Desk, with PTI), 9 December 2019

Newslaundry quotes an unnamed police officer and a DCP (by designation) and does not say who ordered either lathicharge. A police officer is quoted saying the students lacked permission to march to Rashtrapati Bhavan; whether permission was sought or refused is not stated in any page read. notes: Search of news coverage only; Delhi Police FIR portal not searched.

claim: Delhi High Court, single judge (Justice Rajiv Shakdher), 24 January 2020, on a petition by the JNU Students' Union through its president and office bearers challenging the October 2019 hostel manual changes: JNU was to register students not yet registered for the winter session at the old hostel charges without late fee, and to respond to the petition; next hearing 28 February 2020. The Central government and the University Grants Commission are parties.
